The handoff is the product

Automation succeeds or fails in the handoffs between machines, systems, and people, and that is exactly where product management earns its keep. A conveyor or a robot is a component. The product is the whole flow, working at rate, on a bad day, with a real crew.

The brand system

I never show up alone

Authority is not a title, it is a system. Mine has three parts, and it runs every week: outreach that carries proof, a deliberate path into the right rooms, and a voice that sounds like the operator behind the results. Select each part to see how it works.

Plus One: every message brings its proof

Most outreach asks for attention. Plus One earns it. Every introduction, pitch, and cold note I send carries a plus one: a number, a result, or a story from the floor that the reader can verify. It is the difference between claiming expertise and demonstrating it.

How it runs

  • One proof point per message, chosen for that reader
  • Introductions written so a stranger can forward them in ten seconds
  • Follow ups that add a new fact, never just a nudge

In practice

I build warehouse automation products. I have deployed Dematic conveyors and Locus Robotics AMRs at Walmart scale. If you are weighing an automation investment, I have opinions and receipts. The Plus One standard: claim, number, invitation

Booker: rooms are a pipeline too

Speaking slots, panels, podcasts, and advisory conversations do not arrive by accident. Booker treats them like a product pipeline: a target list of rooms where operators and executives decide budgets, a point of view worth inviting, and steady follow through.

The rooms that matter

  • Warehouse automation conferences and panels
  • Automation and product leadership podcasts and operator roundtables
  • Executive rooms where automation roadmaps get funded

Signature talks

  • Warehouse automation is a product: roadmaps from the floor up
  • Automation ROI without the fairy tales
  • Conveyors or AMRs: choosing the automation that fits your floor

Main Character: five rules, one voice

A personal brand fails when the writing sounds like everyone else. Main Character is my voice, written down as five rules, so a post, a talk, or a proposal all sound like the same person: the operator who has stood on the floor and read the P&L.

The five rules

  • Lead with the decision, then the reason
  • Numbers before adjectives, always
  • One anchor sentence per room, per post, per talk
  • Floor first: if it fails on the floor, it does not ship
  • Close with the ask, the owner, and the date

What it produces

  • LinkedIn writing on warehouse product and leadership
  • Talks built around one decision the audience can reuse
  • Advisory work that reads like it was written by a person

Advisory & consulting

Operator advice for teams betting on warehouse automation

I am building an independent advisory practice for leaders investing in warehouse automation: the conveyor, AMR, and automation roadmap questions I answer as an operator, offered to teams who need someone who has deployed this equipment in the room, not another slide deck.

Where this stands: the advisory practice opens in 2027. Right now the door is open for speaking, panels, mentoring, and problem solving conversations. If your question cannot wait, start it on LinkedIn and we will find the right shape for it.
01

Automation product strategy & roadmaps

Automation roadmaps sequenced by expected business outcome: which processes to automate first, which to leave manual, and in what order. Built with engineering on value and ROI, the way I run my own portfolio.

02

Automation decisions without the fairy tales

Conveyors, AMRs, and the systems around them, evaluated on throughput, labor, and the handoffs where automation projects quietly succeed or fail. Vendor neutral, floor tested.

03

Automation readiness diagnostics

A focused read on your floor before you commit capital: where volume and flow justify automation, where they do not, and the size of the prize before you sign with a vendor.

04

Advisory days & pilots

Short, senior, and specific: a day inside your operation and your data, or a scoped automation pilot with a measurable outcome, before anyone signs up for a transformation.

Phase 1

Diagnose

Walk the floor, read the data, find where time and money actually leak.

Phase 2

Roadmap

Rank the fixes by expected outcome and cost, with engineering at the table.

Phase 3

Pilot

Prove the biggest claim small, in one site, against a number agreed up front.

Phase 4

Scale

Roll out what the pilot proved, with the operating rhythm to keep the gains.

The voice, written down

Five rules keep everything under this name consistent, from a LinkedIn post to a boardroom roadmap review.

  1. Decision first Say what you recommend before you explain why.
  2. Numbers before adjectives If it cannot be counted, it is a hope, not a claim.
  3. One anchor sentence Every room and every post gets one line people can repeat.
  4. Floor first If it fails for the people doing the work, it fails.
  5. Close with ownership The ask, the owner, and the date, every time.

The journey

Engineer first. Operator second. Product leader by conviction.

The path matters because it explains the point of view: I came up through production floors and operations, so my product instincts start with how work actually gets done.

  1. Mumbai

    Production engineering, and a first career in industry

    BS in Production Engineering from the University of Mumbai, followed by early career years with Siemens in Mumbai. The floor teaches you what software people forget: work has a physical cost.

  2. 2017

    Move to the US, MS at UT Arlington

    MS in Industrial Engineering at the University of Texas at Arlington. Business analyst work became product ownership, and product ownership became a career.

  3. Ops years

    Operations at Amazon, product at UPS

    Time inside Amazon operations, then product and digital transformation work at UPS in 2021. Seeing fulfillment from the operator seat and the product seat, in the same career, is the whole advantage.

  4. Walmart

    Warehouse automation at the largest scale

    Warehouse automation product work in Walmart fulfillment operations: deploying Dematic automated conveyor systems and Locus Robotics autonomous mobile robots on live floors.

  5. Today

    Principal Product Manager, Gordon Food Service

    I lead a team of two product owners and build portfolio roadmaps the business plans against, with the operator's eye for automation I brought from the floor up.

  6. 2027 →

    The advisory practice, and what comes after

    Independent consulting in warehouse automation product, built on the record above. The long game is the same as the short one: own real outcomes, in real operations, and let the results compound into a name people trust.
